docs.presetsLayouts.component: The arrangements a game actually reaches for, one page per walk: the `row` opened up to its
cross-axis and its other direction, a `grid`, prepared `slots`, and a `radial` circle. Every
one is an ORDINARY FUNCTION the kit exports, returning the same still-nameless RECORD
`rowLayout` does — and the `registerLayout` call in every stand here is made in front of you
on purpose, because that call is the one move a game repeats for each arrangement of its own:
import { Container, gridLayout, node, registerLayout } from "game-kit"
Two laws hold on every page of this shelf. Spacing and alignment are parameters of the RECORD,
never fields of the node — `gap` means something in a row and nothing in a free layout, and a
field four arrangements out of five cannot use is a field that gets misread. And a layout's
answer is POINTS and nothing else, by type: no walk here can turn a card, lift it, or scale it.
A seat in the circle that should face the middle says so with the child's own `angle`.
The cards on these stands are sized differently on purpose: alignment is invisible over equal
boxes, and a row of equal cells would pass off `start`, `center` and `end` as one picture.
docs.presetsLayouts.row: The stock walk with its cross-axis opened up. `align` says which edges line up across the
line: `start` is tops, `end` is bottoms, `center` — the default, and the stock record's only
answer — the middles. Flip through all three and watch the seams: the walk along the line
never spends a unit, alignment moves cards only across it.
`start`/`end` are named for SCREEN edges, not for reading order: y runs down here, exactly as
in `Atoms/Transformable`, so `start` presses tops level the way a shelf presses books.
docs.presetsLayouts.column: The same walk down the other axis — `direction` is a parameter of the record, not a second
preset. The walk now reads HEIGHTS, the gap stands between vertical neighbours, and `align`
turned with the line: `start` means left edges now, because it names the edge that lines up,
and the edge that can line up is always across the walk.
docs.presetsLayouts.grid: Cells in reading order, left to right first, centred on the container's origin. A track fits
its largest member — the column with the widest card is that wide for every row it crosses —
rather than cutting anyone to a constant cell.
A cell is an ADDRESS: five cards on three columns leave the last row partial, under the first
columns, not recentred. A card that moves when its neighbour leaves is a card the reader
`justifyItems` and `alignItems` place a card WITHIN its cell — across and down — and spend no
track space doing it. Shrink one card and press it into a corner of its cell: every other
card, and every track line, holds still.
docs.presetsLayouts.slots: Prepared places, taken in tree order: seat one goes to the first child, a board drawn before
anyone sits down. The slots are data in the record — move one and its occupant follows on the
next frame, whoever that occupant is by then.
This stand seats one card MORE than there are slots, on purpose. The guest beyond the last
slot is answered `undefined`, so its own pose stands — exactly the `free` answer — and the
seated cards do not shuffle to absorb it. Six seats and a seventh guest is a content
docs.presetsLayouts.radial: Seats on a circle — players around a table, options around a wheel. Degrees run clockwise
from twelve o'clock, the same sense `Transformable.angle` turns, so `startAngle: 90` stands
the first card on the right of the screen.
The full 360 shares the circle evenly with NO doubled seat at the seam: four guests sit at
quarter turns, not at 0°, 120°, 240° and 360°-which-is-0° again. Pull `sweep` under 360 and
the walk becomes an arc taken end to end — the fan's fencepost, not the circle's.
And the seat is a POINT. No card here faces the middle, whatever the count, because a place
